identity.title: POCUS: anechoic dependent pleural collection with spine sign / lung flapping

technique.how: Curvilinear or phased-array probe in the posterior axillary line at the diaphragm (FAST RUQ/LUQ views); find the diaphragm and liver/spleen. Effusion = anechoic or hypoechoic dependent space above the diaphragm bounded by chest wall, with the lung base floating or flapping in it; the thoracic spine visible above the diaphragm (spine sign) confirms fluid.
technique.prerequisites: Patient supine or sitting; scan both bases and compare sides.
technique.contraindications: None; dressings or subcutaneous emphysema limit the window.

interpretation.positive_finding: An anechoic dependent collection with spine sign identifies pleural effusion with pooled specificity 0.98 and LR+ ~54 against CT/surgery; bilateral effusions favour heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome, unilateral favours parapneumonic or malignant effusion.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal scan of both bases makes a clinically important effusion unlikely (pooled sensitivity 0.94, LR- 0.06), better than supine chest radiography (sensitivity 0.51).
interpretation.pitfalls: Mirror-image artefact of the liver above the diaphragm can be mistaken for fluid; complex septated or echogenic effusions (empyema, hemothorax) are less anechoic. Ascites below the diaphragm and a raised hemidiaphragm are confusers.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: characterise size and laterality, consider diagnostic thoracentesis; negative: remove effusion from the dyspnea differential and look for other causes.

sources.citation: Yousefifard M, Baikpour M, Ghelichkhani P, Asady H, Shahsavari Nia K, Moghadas Jafari A, Hosseini M, Safari S. Screening Performance Characteristic of Ultrasonography and Radiography in Detection of Pleural Effusion; a Meta-Analysis. Emerg (Tehran). 2016.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a single anterior or supine view; small effusions are posterior and dependent and need a lateral/posterior window.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Large effusion with hypoxia, hypotension, or fever needs urgent drainage assessment; unilateral effusion with sepsis suggests empyema.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Sensitivity was higher with radiologist/intensivist operators (0.97) than other physicians (0.90); specificity was unaffected by operator (Table 2). No kappa reported.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Basic thoracic POCUS competence (FAST-level views of both bases); studies used intensivists, radiologists, emergency physicians, internists and trained nurses with 1-10 MHz probes.

extraction_notes: Pooled sens/spec and LR entries are split into two estimate rows because a single verbatim quote containing all four numbers with CIs exceeds the quote cap; they describe the same 12-study analysis. Table 2 prints the radiologist/intensivist sensitivity as '0.97 (0.83-0.96)', an internally inconsistent CI (the same CI as the 'other physician' row), so CI is left null for that entry. Sonographic definitions varied across the 12 primary studies (anechoic dependent collection with or without spine sign/lung flapping); the meta-analysis did not require the spine sign, so the title's refinement is a bedside confirmation feature rather than the pooled threshold. Prevalence not entered: pooled counts (646/1558 hemithoraces or patients, mixed designs) are not a single cohort prevalence. Pocket-size device sensitivity ranged 62-98% in three small studies (Discussion). Comparator: chest radiography pooled sensitivity 0.51 (0.33-0.68), specificity 0.91 (0.68-0.98) (Abstract).
